title: Role of community health workers in improving cost efficiency in an active case finding tuberculosis programme: an operational research study from rural Bihar, India
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cost-efficient active case finding (ACF) approaches are needed for their large-scale adoption in national tuberculosis (TB) programmes. Our aim was to assess if community health workers' (CHW) knowledge about families' health status can improve the cost efficiency of the ACF programme without adversely affecting the delivery of other health services for which they are responsible. DESIGN: Quasi-experimental design. INTERVENTIONS: We evaluated an ACF programme in the Samastipur district in Bihar, India, between July 2017 and June 2018. CHWs called Accredited Social Health Activists generated referrals of individuals at risk of TB and conducted symptom-based screening to identify patients with presumptive TB. They also helped them undergo testing and provided treatment support for confirmed TB cases. PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: We compared the notification rate from the intervention region with that from a control region in the same district with similar characteristics. We analysed operational data to calculate the cost per TB case diagnosed. We used routine programmatic data from the public health system to estimate the impact on other services provided by CHWs. FINDINGS: CHWs identified 9895 patients with presumptive TB. Of these, 5864 patients were tested for TB, and 1236 were confirmed as TB cases. Annual public case notification rate increased sharply in the intervention region from 45.8 to 105.8 per 100 000 population, whereas it decreased from 50.7 to 45.3 in the control region. There was no practically or statistically significant impact on other output indicators of the CHWs, such as institutional deliveries (-0.04%). The overall cost of the intervention was about US$134 per diagnosed case. Main cost drivers were human resources, and commodities (drugs and diagnostics), which contributed 37.4% and 32.5% of the cost, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ACF programmes that use existing CHWs in the health system are feasible, cost efficient and do not adversely affect other healthcare services delivered by CHWs.

summary.oneLiner: Using existing community health workers to actively find TB cases in rural Bihar was feasible, cost-efficient, and did not harm their other health services.
summary.overview: Active case finding means health workers go out to look for tuberculosis (TB) cases instead of waiting for patients to come to clinics. This study tested whether community health workers called ASHAs, who already handle other rural health duties, could do this cost-efficiently in Samastipur district, Bihar, India, over one year. The authors compared an intervention region with a control region in the same district, and found that officially reported TB cases rose sharply in the intervention region while falling slightly in the control region. The programme cost about US$134 per diagnosed case, and the authors found no practically or statistically significant effect on other services such as institutional deliveries. The study is a quasi-experimental design, so the comparison is not randomised.
summary.question: Can community health workers' knowledge of families' health status improve the cost efficiency of an active case finding programme for TB, without adversely affecting the other health services they provide?
summary.method: Quasi-experimental design comparing the public case notification rate in an intervention region with that in a similar control region in the same district. Operational data were analysed to calculate the cost per TB case diagnosed, and routine programmatic data from the public health system were used to estimate the impact on other services delivered by the health workers.
summary.data: Active case finding programme in Samastipur district, Bihar, India, run between July 2017 and June 2018. Community health workers identified 9895 patients with presumptive TB, 5864 of whom were tested, and 1236 were confirmed as TB cases.
findings: Annual public case notification rate in the intervention region rose sharply from 45.8 to 105.8 per 100 000 population.
In the control region, the notification rate decreased from 50.7 to 45.3 per 100 000 population over the same period.
No practically or statistically significant impact was found on other output indicators of the community health workers, such as institutional deliveries (-0.04%).
The overall cost of the intervention was about US$134 per diagnosed case.
Human resources (37.4%) and commodities such as drugs and diagnostics (32.5%) were the main cost drivers.
The authors conclude that active case finding programmes using existing community health workers are feasible, cost efficient and do not adversely affect other health services those workers deliver.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest that large-scale active case finding in national TB programmes can be cost-efficient when it uses community health workers already in the health system, without reducing their other services. Human resources and drugs and diagnostics are the main cost items to plan around.
